text: Your microwave doesn't cook from the outside in. Not really. It shakes your food. So why is the edge lava hot while the middle is still cold?
A part called a magnetron makes radio waves about twelve centimeters long, and fires them into a metal box. Metal reflects them, so the waves bounce back and forth.
Water molecules have a plus end and a minus end. The wave flips back and forth billions of times a second, and the molecules wiggle and rub against each other. That friction is heat.
But the bouncing waves overlap into a standing pattern. Some spots get strong pushes, others almost none. That's why a turntable spins your food through the hot and cold spots.
Quick test. Why does the plate spin? A, to stir the food. B, to move it through the hot spots. Or C, just for show? Think!

B. The pattern stays put, and the plate moves the food through it. Fun trick: melt a chocolate bar, measure the gap between the melted spots, double it, multiply by two point four five billion, and you get the speed of light.
Two tips. Stir halfway, then let food stand a minute so the heat spreads inward. And never overheat plain water in a smooth cup. It can superheat and erupt. Use short bursts.
Watch again, and count the hot spots.
